questions.question: Why do atoms form bonds rather than remaining isolated? Frame the answer in energy terms.
questions.solution: Bonding LOWERS the total energy: shared or transferred electrons let both atoms reach a more stable arrangement (filled valence shell, lower PE), and the released energy appears as bond formation enthalpy. Isolated atoms are not at minimum energy; bonds are the path downhill. Stability = lower energy, not 'satisfaction of rules' alone.

questions.question: Why is the mole called chemistry's 'counting bridge' between the invisible and the weighable?
questions.solution: Atoms are too small to count individually; the mole (6.022×10²³ particles) converts a COUNT of particles into a MASS you can weigh on a balance — 1 mol of C-12 weighs exactly 12 g. Every stoichiometric calculation crosses this bridge: mass → moles → particles (or reacting moles) → mass.

questions.question: A compound is 40% C, 6.7% H, 53.3% O with molar mass 180. Find both formulas and explain the role of the molar mass.
questions.solution: Moles: C 40/12 = 3.33, H 6.7/1 = 6.7, O 53.3/16 = 3.33 → ratio 1 : 2 : 1 → empirical CH₂O (mass 30). Molecular formula = (molar mass/empirical mass) × empirical = (180/30) × CH₂O = C₆H₁₂O₆ (glucose). The molar mass tells HOW MANY empirical units sit in one molecule — without it the answer is a family (CH₂O, C₂H₄O₂, …).

questions.question: 3 mol H₂ react with 3 mol O₂ (2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O). Which is limiting and how much water forms? Explain the logic, not just the arithmetic.
questions.solution: The reaction consumes H₂ : O₂ in ratio 2 : 1; 3 mol H₂ needs only 1.5 mol O₂, so H₂ runs out first — H₂ is limiting. Water formed = 3 mol (all the H₂ is used). The limiting reagent is whichever runs out FIRST per the stoichiometric ratio; the excess reagent's leftover (1.5 mol O₂) is irrelevant to yield.

questions.question: Find the oxidation number of S in H₂SO₄ and of Cr in Cr₂O₇²⁻, and state the rule being applied.
questions.solution: H₂SO₄: 2(+1) + S + 4(−2) = 0 → S = +6. Cr₂O₇²⁻: 2Cr + 7(−2) = −2 → Cr = +6. Rule: the sum of oxidation numbers equals the species' charge (0 for neutral). Oxygen is −2 (except peroxides), hydrogen +1 (except hydrides) — the fixed anchors make the unknown solvable.

questions.concept: Why the mole counts particles, not mass
questions.question: One mole of H₂O and one mole of H₂SO₄ have wildly different masses yet the same number of formula units. Why is the mole defined on count?
questions.solution: Chemical reactions happen particle-to-particle, in fixed ratios, so the useful bookkeeping unit must be a COUNT. The mole is just Avogadro's number of particles, with molar mass as the conversion to grams: n = m/M. Reactions balance in moles, not grams — that is why stoichiometry is done in moles.

questions.concept: Why the limiting reagent controls the yield
questions.question: In a reaction you have excess of one reactant and a shortfall of the other. Why is the shortfall reactant the one that controls the product amount?
questions.solution: Product forms only where BOTH reactants are available in the stoichiometric ratio; once the scarce reagent is exhausted, pairing stops no matter how much of the other remains. So the product amount is set by moles of the limiting reagent, divided by its coefficient. The excess reagent is left over, not 'unused capacity' — its presence changes nothing. Identify the limiting reagent first, always.

questions.concept: Why significant figures matter in analysis
questions.question: Why does reporting an atomic mass as 12.0110 g/mol from a balance reading 12.01 g misrepresent the measurement?
questions.solution: The reported precision cannot exceed the measurement's precision. A reading of 12.01 g supports four significant figures, so extra trailing digits are fabricated certainty. Significant figures encode the reliability of the instrument, so carrying them beyond it misleads the reader about error. Report to the weakest measured precision.
